growth_story.headline: Bolivia's gas boom drove growth until 2017; as gas output fell and dollars and fuel ran short, income per person slid back to its 2014 level.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2017 Bolivia's income per person grew 2.4 percent a year, and faster in the decade to 2015, at 3.3 percent a year, as high world prices for natural gas and minerals raised export and tax revenues. The IMF credits the years 2006 to 2014 with large economic and social gains, as higher gas revenues paid for more infrastructure and wider social programs. When gas and mineral prices fell in 2014, the government kept spending to hold up growth, so income per person still rose 2.7 percent in both 2016 and 2017, while deficits widened and reserves fell. Since 2018 growth has averaged -0.6 percent a year: income per person peaked in 2019, fell 13.8 percent in 2020, and after a rebound shrank again in 2024 and 2025 as gas output kept falling and dollars and fuel ran short. By 2025 it was 7.8 percent below its 2019 peak, about where it first was in 2014, and the last decade averaged 0.0 percent a year.

threads.title: The gas boom years
threads.text: High prices for natural gas and minerals raised government revenue in the boom years. The state spent much of it on infrastructure and social programs, and income per person grew 3.3 percent a year over 2006 to 2015.

since_last_year.text: Since December 2025 the government has adjusted domestic fuel prices, frozen public wages and hiring, and cut public investment. In June 2026 it moved toward a flexible exchange rate, and in July 2026 it reached a staff-level agreement with the IMF on a loan program that still needs approval by the IMF's Executive Board. The World Bank expects output to shrink again in 2026 as spending cuts and tighter money weigh on demand.

growth_story.tension: The sources date the turn to 2014, when the commodity boom ended, but the data show no break until 2018: public spending kept income per person growing 2.7 percent a year in 2016 and 2017. And the boom growth the IMF reports for 2006 to 2014 is for the whole economy; income per person grew more slowly, 3.3 percent a year over 2006 to 2015, because the population grew too.
